headline: Conflict is inevitable when different people with different needs interact—the question is how we handle it
universal_truth: Disagreement isn't failure; it's information; how you disagree matters more than whether you disagree
fun_facts: Research shows couples who can disagree constructively have stronger relationships than those who avoid conflict
Teams with healthy conflict produce more creative solutions than teams with false harmony
Most conflicts are about unmet needs or miscommunication, not genuine value differences
discussion_questions: How do you typically handle disagreement?
When has conflict led to something positive?
What makes some conflicts constructive and others destructive?

hook.script: Wherever people gather, conflict follows. Different needs, different views, different priorities—friction is inevitable. But conflict isn't inherently bad. Some disagreements clear the air. Some lead to better ideas. The question isn't if you'll conflict, but how.

cliff.script: We often try to avoid conflict, treating it as failure. But suppressed conflict doesn't disappear—it festers. What's the difference between destructive and constructive conflict?

options.text: Constructive conflict focuses on issues rather than people, seeks understanding before agreement, and aims for resolution rather than victory
options.response: Yes. Constructive conflict attacks problems, not people. It's curious before it's certain. It aims to solve, not to win. The goal is mutual understanding, even without agreement.

options.text: Constructive conflict is when you eventually agree
options.response: Agreement is nice, but constructive conflict can end with respectful disagreement...

fact1.title: Issue vs Person
fact1.script: Destructive conflict attacks people: 'You're wrong, you're stupid, you're bad.' Constructive conflict attacks issues: 'This approach has problems.' The same disagreement becomes either relationship-damaging or problem-solving depending on the target.

fact2.title: Understand First
fact2.script: Most conflicts stem from misunderstanding—assumptions about what the other person means or wants. Before arguing, seek to understand. 'What are you actually concerned about?' often dissolves apparent conflict into shared problem-solving.

fact3.title: Conflict Avoidance Cost
fact3.script: Avoiding conflict feels peaceful but creates problems. Resentment builds. Issues go unaddressed. Passive aggression replaces honest disagreement. The short-term comfort of avoidance creates long-term dysfunction.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Disagreement isn't failure; it's information. How you disagree matters more than whether you disagree. Learn to fight well.

outro.script: That's Day 203. Tomorrow, we'll explore what peace actually means. Until then, in your next disagreement, try understanding before arguing.

growTrack.title: Conflict Practice - Understand First
growTrack.activity: In your next disagreement, before responding, ask: 'Can you help me understand your concern?' Listen without defending. Often what seems like opposition is actually a different way of looking at a shared goal.
